titleText.es: LOS ESTUDIANTES ESTÁN LLAMANDO AL PRESIDENTE JOHNSON EN MASA PARA PROTESTAR POR EL BOMBARDEO Y HAN COLAPSADO LA CENTRALITA DE LA CASA BLANCA.¿PODRÍAN COLAPSAR NUESTROS SISTEMAS TELEFÓNICOS CRÍTICOS? ¿HA COMENZADO LA PRIMERA GUERRA TELEFÓNICA? PERMANEZCAN A LA ESCUCHA PARA SABER MÁS SOBRE ESTA NUEVA Y PELIGROSA TECNOLOGÍA.
titleText.en: STUDENTS ARE CALLING PRESIDENT JOHNSON EN MASSE TO PROTEST THE BOMBING AND IT'S JAMMED THE WHITE HOUSE SWITCHBOARD. COULD THEY COLLAPSE OUR CRITICAL PHONE SYSTEMS? HAS THE FIRST TELEPHONE WAR BEGUN? STAY TUNED FOR MORE ON THIS DANGEROUS NEW TECHNOLOGY.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and English texts are the exact title attributes from the Spanish archive and official xkcd. The browser URL, organization names, acronym, personal name, and leading punctuation reaction are audited exclusions. Window controls, navigation icons, the download icon, search icon, globe, figures, and speech tails are structural artwork. Leak remains a lexical English borrowing inside the Spanish phrase NUEVO LEAK.

regions.labelEs: SOMOS ANONYMOUS. SOMOS LEGIÓN. NO SOMOS NADIE Y SOMOS TODOS.

excludedUnits.rationale: This unchanged organization name is excluded while the surrounding Spanish is taught.

applications.explanationEn: Somos gives the group's claimed identity; the printed organization name supplies that identity.
Somos introduces a defining collective description, and legión supplies it.
Somos carries the identity statement, while nadie supplies the deliberately paradoxical description.
Because nadie follows the verb, Spanish keeps no before somos too.
Somos introduces the collective identity, and standalone todos refers to everyone.

regions.labelEs: Y ESTAMOS AQUÍ PARA LUCHAR POR WIKILEAKS.

excludedUnits.rationale: This unchanged organization and website name is excluded while the Spanish construction around it is taught.

applications.explanationEn: Estamos is used for the group's location, and aquí states that location.
Para introduces the purpose, and luchar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
Luchar names the effort and por introduces the cause or organization being supported.

The borrowed noun leak is treated as masculine singular here, so nuevo uses masculine singular -o.

This unchanged organization name is excluded while the surrounding Spanish is taught.

This printed personal name is excluded while the Spanish exclamation is taught.

applications.explanationEn: Maldita and sea work together as the fixed exclamation of anger or frustration.

cards.answerEn: we are (an identity or defining description)
cards.noteEn: Somos is the present form of ser used with nosotros or nosotras, “we.” Ser presents an identity, category, or defining description; estamos normally presents a state or location instead.

example.en: We are neighbors.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.noteEn: A legión was originally a large military unit. It can also describe a very numerous, organized, or devoted group.

example.es: Una legión de seguidores esperaba fuera.
example.en: A legion of followers was waiting outside.

cards.promptEs: legión · nadie y todos · leak de identidades · maldita sea
cards.questionEn: Why is the published leak especially damaging to the Anonymous speaker?
cards.answerEn: The group presents itself as a vast anonymous collective, but the leak publishes members' identifying and contact information.
cards.noteEn: Anonymous became associated with collective slogans and concealed individual identities. WikiLeaks became known for publishing leaked material. The page therefore turns the transparency model against Anonymous itself, and the final speaker identified as Julian reacts in frustration.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nadie is commonly translated as “anyone.” Spanish uses negative concord, so no and nadie can appear together.

example.en: I don’t know anyone.

cards.noteEn: Standalone todos can refer to all the people in a group. It is masculine plural for an all-male or mixed group; todas is used for an all-female group.

example.en: Everyone understood the warning.

cards.answerEn: we are (at a place or location)
cards.noteEn: Estamos is the form of estar used with nosotros, ‘we.’ Use it for where a group is; somos instead gives an identity or defining description.

example.en: We have been here since early.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.promptEs: luchar por + causa, persona u objetivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone fights for or works hard in support of a cause or goal?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of luchar, then por, then name the cause, person, or goal.
cards.noteEn: Por introduces what the effort supports or seeks to defend. If the goal is an action, luchar por can instead be followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.es: Luchan por la libertad de expresión.
example.en: They fight for freedom of expression.

cards.answerEn: to; toward the goal of (after luchar)
cards.noteEn: After luchar, por can introduce the goal being pursued. When that goal is an action, natural English often uses “to” rather than translating por as “for.”

example.en: I strive to learn more.

cards.promptEs: una nueva persona o cosa · una persona o cosa nueva
cards.questionEn: What difference can the position of nuevo make?
cards.answerEn: Before the person or thing, nuevo often means newly added or newly in that role; after it, nuevo more often stresses that the thing itself is brand-new.
cards.noteEn: Nuevo changes to nueva, nuevos, or nuevas to match what it describes. Una nueva compañera usually means someone who has recently become a coworker or classmate. Una mesa nueva more often means a newly made or unused table. Context can blur the contrast, so this is a common tendency rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: Laura has a new coworker.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: information leak; unauthorized release of information
cards.noteEn: Spanish technology and media writing sometimes borrows English leak informally. It is normally treated as a masculine noun: un leak, el leak.

example.es: El periodista investigó un leak de documentos.
example.en: The journalist investigated a leak of documents.

cards.noteEn: Nombres is the plural of nombre. It can refer to personal names, labels, or the names assigned to things.

example.es: La lista contiene nombres y fechas.
example.en: The list contains names and dates.

cards.noteEn: Direcciones can mean addresses or directions. With names and phone numbers, it refers to contact or location addresses.

example.es: Guardaron las direcciones de los clientes.
example.en: They saved the clients' addresses.

cards.questionEn: How do you say phone number or phone numbers?
cards.answerEn: Use número de teléfono for one and números de teléfono for more than one.
cards.noteEn: Número changes between singular and plural. De teléfono identifies the kind of number and stays unchanged in both forms.

example.en: Write down my phone number.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.noteEn: Teléfono is stressed on lé, which is why it carries a written accent.

example.en: The phone is ringing.

cards.noteEn: Bajar literally means to lower or go down. On websites and in informal technology language, it can mean to download a file; descargar is another common choice.

example.es: Puedes bajar el archivo desde la página.
example.en: You can download the file from the page.

cards.questionEn: Why can a button or menu item use an unchanged dictionary-form verb as an instruction?
cards.answerEn: Spanish interfaces often use a verb's unchanged dictionary form to name the action the control performs.
cards.noteEn: This unchanged form is called the infinitive and usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. It is not addressed to tú or usted here; it functions as a short action label, especially on buttons, menus, notices, and lists of instructions.

example.en: Press 'Send' to send the message.

cards.questionEn: How do you exclaim “Damn it!” when something has gone wrong?
cards.answerEn: Use ¡maldita sea! as a fixed expression of anger or frustration.
cards.noteEn: The words literally resemble “damned be it,” but Spanish speakers use the pair as one exclamation. Sea is a special form of ser used here in a wish-like reaction. The expression can sound strong, so use it with care.

example.en: Damn it! I missed the bus.

cards.answerEn: be; no separate English word in maldita sea
cards.noteEn: Sea is a special form of ser used in wishes and reactions. In the fixed exclamation maldita sea, English normally translates the whole expression rather than this word separately.

example.es: Sea como sea, tenemos que salir.
example.en: Be that as it may, we have to leave.
